assumptions: Initial outreach uses newly obtained opt-ins or otherwise valid consent rather than an inherited customer list.
The platform does not itself perform regulated electrical work.
Installers can fulfill incremental bookings without materially degrading service.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A paid installer pilot showing homeowner conversion, fulfilled-service gross profit, low complaint and opt-out rates, repeat annual demand, CAC payback below six months, and retention after the initial campaign.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Installers often under-monetize installed customer bases, and combining consented outreach, payment, and revenue share addresses more of the workflow than reminders alone.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Lost repeat revenue is legible to installers, but the evidence establishes installed assets rather than homeowner demand for paid preventive maintenance or installer willingness to share revenue.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Monthly fees plus collected-revenue share can produce favorable cash conversion and alignment, though service frequency, conversion, support load, CAC, and the assumed 60-75% contribution margin require pilots.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Installers with 500-5,000 assets are a focused and reachable initial segment, but the serviceable revenue pool per installed system may be modest.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: A managed revenue rail can win a useful installer niche, but CRM vendors, distributors, and installers themselves can reproduce campaigns and payments.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: The workflow can extend across batteries, heat pumps, EV chargers, warranties, inspections, repairs, and distributor-led service programs.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Permissioned response and service benchmarks improve optimization, but installer access is nonexclusive, replaceable, and revocable, with homeowners remaining installer-controlled.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Done-for-you conversion and payment collection tied to revenue is more compelling than software reminders, although value collapses if few systems need recurring paid service.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: The growing installed renewable base creates an accumulating renewal opportunity, but no evidence shows an urgent new purchasing window.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: A family-installer pilot is unusually practical and distributor referrals could scale, provided consent and service capacity are handled correctly.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: A low-capital opt-in pilot fits the founder's skills and part-time constraint; principal risks are GDPR, weak conversion, messy data, and insufficient technicians rather than hard regulation.

highest_value_structural_change: Anchor the offer on mandatory or warranty-preserving service events, with payment routing and portable asset records, rather than relying mainly on optional preventive-maintenance subscriptions.
main_structural_strength: The founder has a credible, low-cost route to test a measurable revenue event while leaving homeowner ownership and physical fulfillment with installers.
primary_score_limiter: It is unproven that residential renewable assets generate enough recurring paid service demand to sustain the proposed pricing and revenue share.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Residential PV systems may require little paid preventive maintenance, and the cited subsidy evidence proves installations rather than annual-plan demand.
